translationRepairs: When Hu Sisun and others formed a conspiracy.
Conflict then arose with Husi Chun and the others.
The source names Husi Chun (斛斯椿), and 釁結 says that conflict arose; the reviewed wording corrects both the romanization and the event.
When Hu Sisun and others formed a conspiracy.
Hostilities arose with Husi Chun and the others.
The literal field repeats the wrong Hu Sisun romanization; 斛斯椿 is Husi Chun, while 釁結 denotes hostilities arising.
整信 is the complete two-character given name Zhengxin. Truncating it to Zheng misidentifies Gao Rui's son.
His son Zheng inherited the succession.
The literal field likewise truncates 整信 and uses an awkward succession formula; the reviewed replacement preserves the full name and 嗣.
His father Gao Fan, courtesy name Feique, was posthumously made grand preceptor by Wei and given the posthumous title Duke Xiaoxuan.
His father Gao Fan, courtesy name Feique, was posthumously made grand commandant by Wei and given the posthumous title Duke Xiaoxuan.
太尉 is Grand Commandant, not Grand Preceptor (太師). The proposed idiomatic repair corrects the office without altering the genealogy.
His father Fan, courtesy name Feique, was posthumously made Grand Preceptor by Wei and given posthumous name Duke Xiaoxuan.
His father Fan, courtesy name Feique, was posthumously appointed Grand Commandant by Wei and given the posthumous title Duke Xiaoxuan.
The literal field makes the same 太尉/太師 substitution. Grand Commandant is the source-supported office.
His mother Lady Shan was enfeoffed lady of the commandery; a daughter was made lady attendant within and entered to serve the empress.
His mother, Lady Shan, was enfeoffed as Lady of the Commandery, appointed Female Palace Attendant, and entered the palace to serve the empress.
Lady Shan remains the grammatical subject: 女侍中 is the office to which she was appointed, not a daughter introduced by 女.
His mother Lady Shan was enfeoffed Lady of the Commandery; a daughter was made Lady Attendant Within and entered to serve the empress.
His mother Lady Shan was enfeoffed as Lady of the Commandery, appointed Female Palace Attendant, and entered to serve the empress.
The source lists Lady Shan's enfeoffment, appointment as 女侍中, and palace service in one subject chain; the literal repair removes the invented daughter.

Erzhu Rong still held Bing Province; Gao Huan meant to attack him and left Yue to guard the capital, promoting him to grand general of the flying cavalry and honorary equal to the three ducal ministers.

Erzhu Zhao still held Bing Province; Gao Huan meant to attack him and left Yue to guard the capital, promoting him to grand general of the flying cavalry and honorary equal to the three ducal ministers.
尒朱兆 is Erzhu Zhao. Erzhu Rong is a different person whose name ends in 榮, so the old English points to the wrong historical figure.

At that time Erzhu Rong still held Bing Province; the High Ancestor was about to attack him and ordered Yue to remain guarding the capital, promoting him to Grand General of the Flying Cavalry and Honorary Equal to the Three Ducal Ministers.

At that time Erzhu Zhao still held Bing Province; the High Ancestor was about to attack him and ordered Yue to remain guarding the capital, promoting him to Grand General of the Flying Cavalry and Honorary Equal to the Three Ducal Ministers.
The literal field repeats the same wrong-person substitution; 尒朱兆 unequivocally names Erzhu Zhao.
In the sixth year, for merit, he was made palace attendant and grand preceptor; other offices unchanged; separately enfeoffed viscount of Xinchang.

In the sixth year, he was rewarded for his merit with appointment as palace attendant and grand commandant; his other offices remained unchanged, and he was separately enfeoffed as Viscount of Xinchang.
太尉 is Grand Commandant, and 別封新昌縣子 separately enfeoffs Gao Yue as Viscount of Xinchang; the reviewed prose preserves both facts.
In the sixth year, for merit he was made Palace Attendant and Grand Preceptor; the rest as before; separately enfeoffed Viscount of Xinchang.
In the sixth year, for merit he was made Palace Attendant and Grand Commandant; the rest as before; separately enfeoffed Viscount of Xinchang.
The literal field must also distinguish 太尉 from 太師. Grand Commandant is the correct office in this appointment sequence.

When Gao Zhan died, several days after the burial Rui, together with Prince of Fenyang Gao Run, Prince of Ande Gao Yanzong, and Yuan Wenyao, memorialized the Last Emperor, saying, "He Shikai should not continue to hold an inner appointment."

When Gao Zhan died, several days after the burial, Rui, together with Prince of Fengyi Gao Run, Prince of Ande Gao Yanzong, and Yuan Wenyao, memorialized the Last Emperor, saying, "He Shikai should not continue to hold an inner appointment."
馮翊 is Fengyi, not Fenyang. The reviewed sentence also restores the comma needed to separate the burial phrase from Rui as subject.

When the Imperial Ancestor died, several days after the burial Rui, together with the Prince of Fenyang Run, the Prince of Ande Yanzong, and Yuan Wenyao, memorialized the Last Emperor, saying, "He Shikai should not continue to hold an inner appointment."

When the Imperial Ancestor died, several days after the burial, Rui, together with the Prince of Fengyi Run, the Prince of Ande Yanzong, and Yuan Wenyao, memorialized the Last Emperor, saying, "He Shikai should not continue to hold an inner appointment."
The prince's title is 馮翊王, Prince of Fengyi. The reviewed literal sentence corrects the place-name and its punctuation.
When Houzhu was defeated at Jinyang, the Empress Dowager returned to the capital by the Tumen Road; an edict put Mai in overall command of troops to escort her.
When Houzhu was defeated at Jin Province, the Empress Dowager returned to the capital by the Tumen Road; an edict put Mai in overall command of troops to escort her.
晉州 is Jin Province, whereas Jinyang is 晉陽. The original English relocates Houzhu's defeat to a different place.
When Houzhu was defeated at Jinyang, the Empress Dowager returned to the capital by the Tumen Road; an edict ordered Mai to take overall command of troops and escort the Empress Dowager.
When Houzhu was defeated at Jin Province, the Empress Dowager returned to the capital by the Tumen Road; an edict ordered Mai to take overall command of troops and escort the Empress Dowager.
The literal field repeats the 晉州/晉陽 confusion; Jin Province is the direct source reading.
Appraisal: Zhao Commandery — heroic and grand; bearing composed, mien upright.
Appraisal: The Prince of Zhao Commandery was heroic and imposing, his bearing composed and upright.
趙郡 is an abbreviated reference to the Prince of Zhao Commandery in this appraisal, not an appraisal of the commandery as a place.
Appraisal: Zhao Commandery — heroic and grand; bearing and mien composed and upright.
Appraisal: The Prince of Zhao Commandery was heroic and imposing; his bearing and mien were composed and upright.
The literal field needs the same personal referent and an expressed English predicate for 風範凝正.
Illustrious Qinghe — by him the state was governed.
Illustrious was the Prince of Qinghe, through whom the state was governed.
清河 abbreviates the Prince of Qinghe. Restoring the title makes the personal praise in 赫赫 and 經國 intelligible in English.
Illustrious Qinghe — by him the state was ordered.
Illustrious was the Prince of Qinghe; through him the state was ordered.
The literal field likewise treats the princely title as a bare place-name; the reviewed sentence preserves the compact parallelism.
A small flaw at the end of the road — not a collapse of virtue.
A minor failing at the end did not ruin his virtue.
末路 denotes the end of Gao Yue's course or career here, not a literal road, and 非為敗德 denies that the flaw destroyed his virtue.
A small stain at the final road — not a ruin of virtue.
A small flaw at the end was not the ruin of his virtue.
The old literal is an ungrammatical calque of 末路 and 敗德; the reviewed wording keeps the contrast while remaining literal.
